title: Learning Cybersecurity with AI
subtitle: A study roadmap with legal practice resources
author: JARVIS
summary:
This report outlines a practical way to learn cybersecurity using AI as a tutor while practising only on systems built for learning. It lists free resources [S1] [S3] [S4] and a suggested six-month plan.

The plan is a recommendation, not an industry standard; map it to the role you want using the NICE Framework [S2].

sections.heading: How AI helps a learner
paragraphs: An AI assistant is most useful as a **patient tutor**: it explains concepts, quizzes you and reviews your own code. It is least useful when treated as an oracle, because it can be confidently wrong.
Check what it says against primary sources such as the OWASP Top Ten [S1] and MITRE ATT&CK [S5].
bullets: Ask for explanations at your level
Ask it to check your reasoning, not to do the work

sections.heading: Practise only where you are allowed
paragraphs: Deliberately vulnerable labs exist so learners can practise legally. PortSwigger's Web Security Academy [S3] and the OverTheWire wargames [S4] are free examples.
sections.callout: Testing a system without written permission can be illegal. Use the lab systems the platforms provide.

table.caption: Free learning resources mentioned in this report.

sections.heading: A suggested six-month plan
paragraphs: The split below is an example for about twelve hours a week. It is a plan, not measured data.
bullets: Months 1-2: networking, Linux, scripting and web fundamentals
Months 3-4: hands-on web labs and detection practice
Months 5-6: threat modelling with ATT&CK [S5] and a portfolio project

sections.heading: What is still uncertain
paragraphs: How well AI tutors improve long-term skill compared with traditional study has not been settled; treat any claim either way with care.
